summary: High-quality course. I recomputed every numeric key and worked example independently in Python (NPV, EAC/CRF, payback, EVM, critical path and float, fault-tree gates, risk scores, EAL, LCA embodied carbon, carbon payback, statistics, RACI workloads) and all keys and tolerances are correct; MCQ keys are single-correct and explanations match the lesson. The UK-SPEC A-E areas, NSPE canons, Engineering Council/RAEng four principles, Gibbs' six stages, Tuckman, HAZOP guide words, ISO 14040/44 phases, the 25-year registered design maximum, life-plus-70 copyright, 20-year patent term, the FE/PE route, and the Hyatt Regency (1981, 114 deaths) and Challenger (73 s) hooks all check out against my knowledge. No literal \uXXXX escapes, '[object Object]' or garbled non-Latin characters were found (the packets are pure ASCII). Only minor issues remain: a few legal paraphrases I could not fully verify (HSWA s.6, Patents Act s.39/s.42), one implausible data value, and small wording inconsistencies. This is an AI review only; the course still needs a subject-matter expert (and for the legal and licensure points, a source check against current statute and awarding-body guidance) before engineering or professional reliance.

issues.problem: Worked example: a premium 5.5 kW motor is said to carry '900 kg CO2e of extra embodied carbon' over a standard motor. A 5.5 kW motor has a mass of a few tens of kg, so the extra material in a premium version would normally be worth tens (not hundreds) of kg CO2e; 94.0% at 5.5 kW is also above typical IE3/IE4 catalogue efficiencies. The arithmetic (payback 2.16 yr, net 4090 kg) is correct, but the inputs look unrealistic (unverified).
issues.suggestedFix: Source-check typical extra embodied carbon and efficiencies for premium-efficiency motors and use realistic values (or label the figures explicitly as illustrative), noting the payback would then be well under a year.

issues.problem: EVM worked example answer says the project is '12% over cost' but the same example forecasts 453 000 GBP against BAC 400 000 GBP (13.3% over); CPI 0.88 implies cost of 1.134 GBP per GBP of work, and 12% is CV/AC, not an overrun against budget.
issues.suggestedFix: Say 'about 13% over cost for the work done' (1/CPI - 1), or state that CPI is 0.88 (12% shortfall in value per GBP spent) without calling it a 12% overrun.

issues.problem: HSWA 1974 s.6 is paraphrased as requiring articles to be 'safe and without risks to health' without the qualifier 'when properly used' (and s.6 is framed around articles being set, used, cleaned or maintained by a person at work). The lesson then attaches 'reasonably foreseeable misuse' and 'transport and disposal' to the duty; these come from negligence law and machinery/design standards (for example ISO 12100), not the s.6 text (unverified against current consolidated wording).
issues.suggestedFix: Check against legislation.gov.uk and state s.6 as: designed and constructed to be safe and without risks to health when properly used, with testing and adequate information; attribute foreseeable misuse to negligence/machinery safety standards.

issues.problem: Ownership table row 'Employee invents outside duties... Generally belongs to the employee, but check the contract / read for assignment clauses' is incomplete for the UK: Patents Act 1977 s.39 splits ownership by duties/special obligations, and s.42 makes contract terms that diminish an employee's rights in inventions belonging to the employee unenforceable. Q010 marking guide ('relatedness to the employer's business', 'company resources') leans on factors that are not the UK s.39 test (unverified, needs legal check).
issues.suggestedFix: Add that, in the UK, s.39 turns on normal/assigned duties and special obligations (senior staff), and that s.42 limits assignment clauses; keep the 'local law varies' caveat and align the Q010 marking guide with the duties-based test.

issues.problem: Worked example calls the control an 'interlocked fixed guard'. Fixed guards (removable only with tools) are not interlocked; interlocking guards are movable guards. The term is contradictory.
issues.suggestedFix: Use 'fixed guard' or 'interlocked movable guard' (the example then needs the guard to stop hazardous motion before access).

issues.problem: Steam-pipe worked example treats the whole 450 W/m loss as saved ('saves about 2400 GBP a year') and quotes payback 1.5 years. Insulating a bare pipe reduces but does not eliminate heat loss, so the saving is overstated (the arithmetic 2430 GBP/yr and 1.48 yr is otherwise correct).
issues.suggestedFix: State an assumption such as 'insulation removes 90% of the loss' and scale saving and payback, or state explicitly that the figure assumes total elimination as an upper bound.

issues.problem: Lesson gives a rule of thumb of 'about one to two minutes per content slide', but the worked example uses 2.5 minutes per evidence slide and q003 uses 3 minutes per content slide.
issues.suggestedFix: Align the rule of thumb with the examples (for example 'one to three minutes per slide, depending on complexity') or state that the figures in the examples are chosen for the arithmetic.

issues.problem: Key (b) says vibration analysis goes first because importance times shortfall 'may still be larger'. No numbers are given, so the correct choice is not determinate; with a sufficiently large shortfall and non-trivial weight on the minor item, (a) could be right.
issues.suggestedFix: Give weights and shortfalls (for example weight 40% shortfall 1 versus weight 5% shortfall 4) so that the weighted gaps can be computed and (b) is unambiguously correct.
